q: The SI unit of angular displacement is the:
x: The radian is the SI unit of angular displacement. Degrees and revolutions also measure angles but are not SI units, and the metre measures length.

q: A particle moves 6 m along the arc of a circle of radius 2 m. Its angular displacement is:
x: θ = s/r = 6/2 = 3 rad. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 12 rad, and dividing the wrong way gives 0.33 rad.

q: The direction of a small angular displacement of a rotating body is:
o: Along the tangent to the circular path
Towards the centre of the circle
Along the axis of rotation, given by the right-hand rule
x: A small angular displacement is a vector along the axis of rotation; curling the fingers of the right hand in the sense of rotation, the thumb gives its direction. The tangent is the direction of linear velocity.

q: A wheel completes 5 revolutions. Its angular displacement is:
x: One revolution is 2π rad, so 5 revolutions are 5 × 2π = 10π rad. 1800 is the angle in degrees, not radians.

q: Points X (near the centre) and Y (near the rim) lie on a rotating rigid disc. In the same time interval:
o: Both travel the same arc length
X has a larger angular displacement than Y
Y has a larger angular displacement than X
Both have the same angular displacement, but Y travels a longer arc
x: Every point of a rigid body turns through the same angle. Arc length s = rθ is larger for Y because it is farther from the axis.

q: The radian has no dimensions because it is defined as the:
o: Ratio of an arc length to the radius
Product of arc length and radius
Ratio of the radius to the time taken
Number of degrees in one revolution
x: θ = s/r is a length divided by a length, so the radian is dimensionless. The other quantities either have dimensions or do not define the radian.

q: Through what angle does the minute hand of a clock turn in 20 minutes?
x: The minute hand makes one revolution (2π rad) in 60 min, so in 20 min it turns ⅓ × 2π = 2π/3 rad.

q: A body moves halfway round a circle of radius 7 m. Its angular displacement and the distance along the arc are (π = 22/7):
x: Half a revolution is π rad, and the arc length is s = rθ = 7 × 22/7 = 22 m. 14 m is the diameter, which is the straight-line displacement, not the arc length.

q: Angular displacement can be treated as a vector quantity only when it is:
x: Very small angular displacements add like vectors; large ones do not obey the vector law of addition, so they are not treated as vectors. The unit or sense of rotation does not decide this.

q: Angular displacement of a body moving in a circle is the:
o: Angle swept out by the radius line in a given time
Straight-line distance between the start and end points
Number of revolutions made per second
x: Angular displacement is the angle through which the radius joining the body to the centre turns. Arc length per second is linear speed, and revolutions per second is frequency.

q: One complete revolution is equal to:
x: In one revolution the arc length is the circumference 2πr, so θ = 2πr/r = 2π rad. π rad is half a revolution.

q: One radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc whose length is equal to the:
x: This is the definition of the radian: arc length equal to the radius gives θ = r/r = 1 rad. An arc equal to the diameter would give 2 rad.

q: One radian is approximately equal to:
x: 1 rad = 180°/π ≈ 57.3°. 180° is π rad, and 3.14 is the value of π, not of one radian in degrees.

q: An angle of 150° expressed in radians is:
An angle of 3π/2 rad is equal to:
x: Degrees = (3π/2) × (180°/π) = 270°, which is three-quarters of a revolution.

q: One degree is equal to:
x: 360° = 2π rad, so 1° = 2π/360 = π/180 rad ≈ 0.0175 rad. 180/π is the number of degrees in one radian.

q: Which shows the angles in correct increasing order of size?
x: 1 rad ≈ 57.3°, which is larger than 1° but smaller than 90°, and 1 revolution is 360°. So the order is 1°, 1 rad, 90°, 1 revolution.

q: The radius of a circle is doubled. In radians, one complete revolution round the new circle is:
x: θ = s/r: doubling r doubles the circumference too, so the ratio stays 2πr/r = 2π rad. The radian measure of an angle does not depend on the size of the circle.

q: An arc whose length equals the diameter of a circle subtends at the centre an angle of:
x: θ = s/r = 2r/r = 2 rad. An arc equal to the radius subtends 1 rad, and π rad needs an arc of half the circumference.

q: Which of the following angles is the largest?
x: 2 rad ≈ 2 × 57.3° ≈ 115°, while 0.25 revolution = 90° and 1.5 rad ≈ 86°. So 2 rad is larger than 100° and the others.

q: The SI unit of angular velocity is:
x: Angular velocity is angular displacement per unit time, so its SI unit is radian per second. rad s⁻² is the unit of angular acceleration, and m s⁻¹ is for linear velocity.

q: A body moving in a circle turns through 180° in 0.5 s. Its average angular velocity is:
x: 180° = π rad, so ω = θ/t = π/0.5 = 2π rad s⁻¹. 360 comes from dividing degrees by time and wrongly calling the result rad s⁻¹.

q: A body moves in a circle at constant speed and completes one revolution every 2 s. Its angular velocity is:
x: ω = 2π/T = 2π/2 = π rad s⁻¹. Multiplying 2π by T instead of dividing gives 4π rad s⁻¹.

q: A disc rotates anticlockwise in a horizontal plane, as seen from above. The direction of its angular velocity is:
o: Along the tangent to the rim
Towards the centre of the disc
x: By the right-hand rule, fingers curled anticlockwise (seen from above) make the thumb point upward along the axis. Angular velocity always lies along the axis of rotation.

q: Taking one rotation of the Earth about its axis as 24 hours, the Earth's angular velocity is:
x: ω = 2π/T with T = 24 × 3600 = 86400 s. 2π/24 is in rad per hour, not per second, and 2π/3600 would mean one turn per hour.

q: A body moves in a circle of radius r with speed v and angular velocity ω. The magnitude of its centripetal acceleration is:
x: Centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = rω², directed towards the centre. v/r is the angular velocity ω, not an acceleration.

q: A 200 g stone tied to a string 50 cm long is whirled in a horizontal circle on a smooth table at a constant speed of 2 m s⁻¹. The tension in the string is:
x: T = mv²/r = 0.2 × 4 / 0.5 = 1.6 N. Leaving r as 50 (cm) gives 0.016 N; using mv/r (forgetting to square v) gives 0.8 N.

q: A body moves in a circle. Its speed is doubled and the radius of its path is also doubled. The centripetal force needed becomes:
x: F = mv²/r: v² becomes 4 times and r becomes 2 times, so F becomes 4/2 = 2 times as large. Ignoring the change in radius gives four times.

q: A 3 kg body moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with a constant angular velocity of 2 rad s⁻¹. The centripetal force on it is:
x: F = mrω² = 3 × 0.5 × 2² = 6 N. Forgetting to square ω gives 3 N; leaving out r gives 12 N.

q: A stone is whirled in a horizontal circle on a string. When the string suddenly breaks, the stone at first moves:
o: Radially outward, away from the centre
Along the tangent to the circle at that point
Along the same circle for a short time
x: Once the string breaks there is no centripetal force, so by Newton's first law the stone continues with its instantaneous velocity, which is along the tangent. Moving radially outward would need an outward force, which does not exist.

q: A 0.5 kg ball on a string 1 m long is whirled in a vertical circle. At the lowest point its speed is 4 m s⁻¹. The tension in the string at the lowest point is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r, so T = 0.5 × 10 + 0.5 × 16 / 1 = 5 + 8 = 13 N. Forgetting the weight gives 8 N; subtracting the weight instead of adding gives 3 N.

q: A body moves in a circle of radius 1 m with a constant period of π s. Its centripetal acceleration is:
x: ω = 2π/T = 2π/π = 2 rad s⁻¹, so a = rω² = 1 × 4 = 4 m s⁻². Forgetting to square ω gives 2 m s⁻².

q: Two small coins, P and Q, lie on a turntable rotating at constant angular velocity, without slipping. P is 10 cm and Q is 30 cm from the axis. The ratio of their centripetal accelerations (P : Q) is:
x: Both have the same ω, so a = rω² ∝ r, giving 10 : 30 = 1 : 3. Using a = v²/r as if the speeds were equal gives 3 : 1.

q: A car rounds a flat (unbanked) circular bend of radius 20 m. The coefficient of static friction between tyres and road is 0.5. The greatest speed at which it can take the bend without skidding is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: Friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r, so v = √(μgr) = √(0.5 × 10 × 20) = √100 = 10 m s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 100 m s⁻¹.

q: A small 2 kg mass is fixed at 0.5 m from an axis of rotation. Treating it as a point mass, its moment of inertia about that axis is:
x: I = mr² = 2 × 0.5² = 2 × 0.25 = 0.5 kg m². Forgetting to square r gives mr = 1 kg m².

q: A thin hoop of mass 2 kg and radius 0.5 m spins about its central axis (perpendicular to its plane) at 4 rad s⁻¹. Its angular momentum is:
x: For a hoop I = mr² = 2 × 0.25 = 0.5 kg m², so L = Iω = 0.5 × 4 = 2 J s. Using the disc formula ½mr² gives 1 J s.

q: A uniform disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m rotates about its central axis at 10 rad s⁻¹. Its moment of inertia is ½mr². Its rotational kinetic energy is:
x: I = ½ × 4 × 0.25 = 0.5 kg m²; K = ½Iω² = ½ × 0.5 × 100 = 25 J. Using I = mr² gives 50 J; dropping both halves gives 100 J.

q: An ice skater spins at 2 rev s⁻¹ with arms outstretched, moment of inertia 4 kg m². She pulls her arms in, reducing her moment of inertia to 1 kg m². Ignoring friction, her new rate of spin is:
x: No external torque, so angular momentum is conserved: I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂, 4 × 2 = 1 × ω₂, ω₂ = 8 rev s⁻¹. Thinking ω falls when I falls gives 0.5 rev s⁻¹.

q: A spinning skater with no external torque pulls in her arms, so her moment of inertia falls to one quarter of its first value. Her rotational kinetic energy:
x: L = Iω is constant, and K = ½Iω² = L²/2I, so when I becomes ¼ of its value K becomes 4 times as large (the extra energy comes from the work she does pulling her arms in). Assuming kinetic energy is conserved, like angular momentum, gives the tempting answer that it stays the same.

q: A uniform disc (I = ½mr²) rolls without slipping along a level floor. What fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?
x: With ω = v/r, rotational K = ½(½mr²)(v/r)² = ¼mv² and translational K = ½mv², so the total is ¾mv² and the rotational fraction is ¼ ÷ ¾ = 1/3. The ratio of rotational to translational energy is 1/2, which is the tempting slip.

q: A uniform disc (I = ½mr²) starts from rest and rolls without slipping down an incline, losing 2.7 m in height. Its speed at the bottom is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: mgh = ½mv² + ½(½mr²)(v/r)² = ¾mv², so v = √(4gh/3) = √(4 × 10 × 2.7 / 3) = √36 = 6 m s⁻¹. Ignoring rotation gives √(2gh) = √54 = 3√6 m s⁻¹; using the hoop result √(gh) gives 3√3 m s⁻¹.

q: A thin hoop and a uniform disc have the same mass and the same radius. About the central axis perpendicular to their planes:
o: The disc has the larger moment of inertia
Both have the same moment of inertia
The hoop has the larger moment of inertia
The larger one depends on how fast they spin
x: All the hoop's mass is at distance r, so I = mr²; the disc's mass is spread from 0 to r, so I = ½mr². The hoop's moment of inertia is twice the disc's; it depends on mass distribution, not on angular speed.

q: The orbital speed of a satellite moving in a circular orbit of radius r around a planet of mass M is:
x: Gravity provides the centripetal force: GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v = √(GM/r). √(2GM/r) is the escape velocity at that distance.

q: A satellite orbits just above the Earth's surface. Taking g = 10 m s⁻² and the Earth's radius as 6.4 × 10⁶ m, its orbital speed is:
x: v = √(gR) = √(10 × 6.4 × 10⁶) = √(6.4 × 10⁷) = 8 × 10³ m s⁻¹ = 8 km s⁻¹. Adding a factor 2 under the root gives the escape velocity, about 11.3 km s⁻¹.

q: A satellite is moved from a circular orbit of radius r to one of radius 4r around the same planet. Its orbital speed becomes:
x: v = √(GM/r) ∝ 1/√r, so making r four times larger makes v 1/√4 = ½ as large. Forgetting the square root gives one quarter.

q: A satellite orbits just above the Earth's surface at 8 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Taking the Earth's radius as 6.4 × 10⁶ m, its period of revolution is:
x: T = 2πR/v = 2π × 6.4 × 10⁶ / 8 × 10³ = 2π × 800 = 1600π s (about 84 minutes). Using πR instead of 2πR gives 800π s.

q: An astronaut inside a satellite orbiting the Earth feels weightless because:
o: There is no gravitational force on her at that height
She and the satellite fall towards the Earth with the same acceleration
The Earth's gravity is cancelled by the Moon's gravity
The air in the satellite holds her up
x: Gravity still acts (it provides the centripetal force), but she and the satellite are both in free fall with the same acceleration, so the floor pushes on her with zero force. Saying gravity is absent is the common wrong idea.

q: A 60 kg man stands on a weighing machine in a lift that is accelerating downward at 2 m s⁻². The reading of the machine, in newtons, is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
x: mg − R = ma, so R = m(g − a) = 60 × 8 = 480 N. Adding the acceleration gives 720 N (the reading for upward acceleration); if a = g the reading would be zero, true weightlessness.

q: A space station is a large ring of radius 40 m rotating about its centre. At what angular velocity must it rotate so that people standing on the inside of the rim feel artificial gravity equal to 10 m s⁻²?
x: The rim must supply centripetal acceleration rω² = g, so ω = √(g/r) = √(10/40) = √0.25 = 0.5 rad s⁻¹. Forgetting the square root gives 0.25 rad s⁻¹; inverting the ratio gives 2 rad s⁻¹.

q: A geostationary satellite, which stays above the same point on the equator, has an orbital period of:
x: To stay above one point it must turn with the Earth, once per rotation of the Earth: 24 hours. 84 minutes is the period of a satellite just above the Earth's surface.
